'''Mordechai "Moti" Segev''' ({{Langx|he|מרדכי "מוטי" שגב}}) is an [[Israel]]i [[physicist]] at the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology|Technion]] who is known for his work on [[laser]]s, [[nonlinear optics]], [[soliton]]s, and [[quantum optics]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mordechai (Moti) Segev |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/mordechai-moti-segev-yyfqqo/ |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref>

== Career ==
Born in [[Romania]] in 1958, Segev emigrated with his family to Israel at the age of 3.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gravé-Lazi |first1=Lidar |title=The power to influence |url=https://www.jpost.com/magazine/features/the-power-to-influence-339835 |website=jpost.com |publisher=[[The Jerusalem Post]] |access-date=October 10, 2025 |date=January 30, 2014}}</ref> He studied physics at the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology]], earning his bachelor's degree in 1985 and his Ph.D. in 1990. After earning his Ph.D., he worked as a [[postdoctoral researcher]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]]. He then went to [[Princeton University]] in 1994 as an assistant professor, and he was promoted to associate professor in 1997 and full professor in 1999. In 1998 Segev returned to work as a professor at the Technion. In 2009 he was appointed the Robert J. Shillman Distinguished Professor of Physics and Electrical Engineering.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Short Biography |url=https://phsites.technion.ac.il/msegev/short-biography/ |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Mordechai (Moti) Segev |language=en-US}}</ref>

In the 1990s, Segev discovered [[Photorefractive effect|photorefractive]] spatial [[soliton]]s<ref>M. Segev, B. Crosignani, A. Yariv, B. Fischer ''Spatial solitons in photorefractive media'', Physical Review Letters 68, 923 (1992).</ref><ref>G. Duree, J. Shultz, G. Salamo, M. Segev, A. Yariv, B. Crosignani, P. DiPorto, E. Sharp, R. R. Neurgaonkar ''Observation of self-trapping of an optical beam due to the photorefractive effect'', Physical Review Letters 71, 533 (1993).</ref> and incoherent solitons (or random-phase solitons).<ref>M. Mitchell, M. Segev ''Self-trapping of incoherent white light'', Nature, Band 387, 1997, S. 880.</ref><ref>M. Mitchell, M. Segev, T. Coskun, D. N. Christodoulides ''Theory of self-trapped spatially-incoherent light beams'', Physical Review Letters 79, 4990 (1997).</ref> He called this the phenomenon of self-trapping in incoherent white light, and he was the first to find solitons in a two-dimensional lattice.<ref>Fleischer, Segev, Efremidis, Christodoulides ''Observation of two dimensional discrete solitons in optically induced nonlinear photonic lattices'', Nature, Band 422, 2003, S. 147</ref><ref>Efremidis,  Hudock, Christodoulides, Fleischer Cohen, Segev ''Two dimensional optical lattice solitons'', Phys. Rev. Lett., Band 91, 2003, S. 213906.</ref> He was also the first to demonstrate [[Anderson localization]] in a perturbed periodic system.<ref>T. Schwartz, G. Bartal, S. Fishman, M. Segev ''Transport and Anderson Localization in disordered two-dimensional Photonic Lattices'', Nature 446, 52 (2007).</ref>

== Honors and awards ==

* 1995-1997 [[Sloan Research Fellowship]]
* 1997 Fellow of [[Optica (society)|Optica]]
* 2000 Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]
* 2007 Quantum Electronics Prize of the [[European Physical Society]]
* 2009 [[Max Born Award]]
* 2011 Member of the [[Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities]]
* 2014 [[Arthur L. Schawlow Prize in Laser Science]]
* 2014 [[Israel Prize]]
* 2015 Elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]]
* 2019 [[EMET Prize]]
* 2021 Elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]
* 2024 [[Rothschild Prize]] in Physics<ref>[[Yad Hanadiv]], [https://www.yadhanadiv.org.il/rothschild-prize The Rothschild Prize]</ref>
